paras: The lynching of Faustine Guitterro was the hanging of a man accused of taking part in the murder of Colonel Charles Potter, whom vigilantes took from the jail at Albuquerque, New Mexico, in late February 1881. Guitterro had been brought in by a sheriff's posse only the night before, according to the wire reports. Papers noted that he was the fourth person put to death without trial for the Potter killing, after three men lynched at the same jail a month earlier.

Potter, described as an officer of the United States Geological Survey who had been collecting statistics for the census bureau, left Albuquerque on October 14, 1880, for the New Placer mining camp and was not heard from again. According to a special to the Dallas Herald, Sheriff Armijo of Bernalillo County arrested Escallero Parera in late January 1881, and Parera confessed to having witnessed, though not shared in, the killing. The sheriff recovered Potter's body near Ojo Chilal and captured two more men, Liguel Barrera and a man the dispatch called "a Mexican known as 'California Joe.'"
On the night of January 31, a band of masked men took Parera, Barrera and California Joe from the Albuquerque jail and hanged them from the porch of the building.

A special to the Galveston News dated Albuquerque, February 25, reported that Guitterro, "implicated in the murder of Colonel Potter," had been brought in "last night" by a sheriff's posse. Vigilantes then took him from the jail and hanged him "in the same place where his accomplices were hung some time since," a spot the earlier report had placed at the jail porch. A Santa Fe dispatch of February 26 said he had been taken out of the jail "last night," and two later weekly digests put the hanging on the night of February 25.

The Canton Register attributed the hanging to "a Vigilance Committee." A rewritten version of the dispatch said instead that "a mob of vigilantes took him out and hanged him to a tree," and the Weekly Chillicothe Crisis also placed the hanging at a tree.

No report of an inquest, arrests or prosecution appears in the coverage. The Chicago Daily Tribune's dispatch said his death made "four persons who have been put to death without trial for the crime," and the Weekly Chillicothe Crisis called it "the fourth lynching for participation in this crime."

The news traveled mainly through the Galveston News special, which the Evening Star of Washington and the Alexandria Gazette printed on February 26 and the Savannah Morning News and Knoxville Daily Chronicle carried in the following days. A shorter Albuquerque dispatch dated February 26 appeared the next day in the Chicago Daily Tribune, the Daily Los Angeles Herald and the Arizona Weekly Citizen.

Headlines treated Guitterro's guilt as settled even where the text said only that he was "implicated": the Savannah Morning News ran "Another of Col. Potter's Assassins Lynched," the Indiana State Sentinel "Murderer Lynched," and the Chicago Daily Tribune's column deck "A Fourth Murderer of Col. Potter Hanged by Vigilantes." The Evening Star used the plainer "Lynching in New Mexico," while the Mower County Transcript and the Watertown Republican printed the rewritten dispatch under the heading "Mexican Justice" (rendered "Mexico Justice" in the Transcript).

In March a one-sentence brief in news digests from Tennessee, Arkansas, Missouri, Indiana and Louisiana identified the victim only by ethnicity and a different name, as "A Mexican named Marino" or "Mario," "another of the alleged murderers of Col. Potter."

The victim's name varies from paper to paper: Faustine Guitterro in the Galveston special, Faustina Guittero in the Chicago Daily Tribune, Fantino Guitterres in the Santa Fe dispatch, and "Marino" or "Mario" in the March digest brief.

The original wire placed the hanging where the earlier victims had died, which the Dallas Herald had described as the jail porch, while the rewritten dispatch and the Weekly Chillicothe Crisis said he was hanged "to a tree"; the wire text is the earlier and closer source. The Galveston special was dated February 25, which would place the hanging the night before, but the Santa Fe dispatch of February 26 and two weekly digests placed it on the night of February 25.

reader.title: Lynching of Faustine Guitterro
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: Vigilantes took an accused man from the Albuquerque jail and hanged him without trial (A4, A7, A16).

Guitterro was taken from jail by 'the vigilantes' or 'a Vigilance Committee' and hanged, one of four 'put to death without trial' for the Potter murder (A4, A7, A16); the group's size is not given, but every report describes a plural body of vigilantes acting on a murder accusation.
The Galveston News special (A4), a separate Albuquerque dispatch of February 26 (A7, A9) and a Santa Fe dispatch (A14) agree that vigilantes took him from the Albuquerque jail and hanged him.

framing.detail: Most papers ran the Galveston special or the Albuquerque dispatch verbatim under headlines such as 'Lynching in New Mexico' and 'Hanged by Vigilantes'.

Headlines presumed guilt ('Another of Col. Potter's Assassins Lynched', 'Murderer Lynched') where the text said only 'implicated', while the Chicago Tribune dispatch noted the four were 'put to death without trial'.
Digest items ran one sentence among other crimes, one identifying him as 'A Mexican named Marino' and another heading the rewrite 'Mexico [Mexican] Justice'.
